chapters.summary: Chair Gale Brewer introduces the hearing on the pied-à-terre tax implementation, noting the confusion around the city's rollout and the Department of Finance publishing a list of 900,000 properties potentially subject to the tax, far exceeding estimates of 14,000.
chapters.title: Chair Brewer opens oversight hearing on pied-à-terre tax rollout

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I am Gail Brewer, the chair of the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Local, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to thank all the members of the public who have joined us today, as well as colleagues, the indomitable, fabulous chair of finance,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: the Linda Lee, Council Member Jay Sanchez, Hanks Wong, Narcis Carmarano, and I think on Zoom we have Palladino.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Today, it's a very strange sort of hearing, but we will conduct oversight of the rollout of the pied-a-terre tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The most recent state budget included a surcharge on property that does not serve as a primary residence, but is more commonly referred to as a pied-à-terre.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There has been a lot of confusion around the city's rollout of the pied-à-terre tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: First, the Department of Finance published on its website a list of around 900,000 residents that it said could potentially be subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Even though the controller estimated in June that less than 14,000 properties would be subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No estimate of the number of peditaires in the city comes even close to 900,000.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yet the city still published the list

chapters.summary: Brewer explains that the published list was so overbroad it included her own name despite her living in the same home since 1994. She questions why DOF published names and addresses when it knew most properties were not pied-à-terres.
chapters.title: Brewer details problems with the 900,000-property published list

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: with the small caveat that the properties on the list may be subject to the charge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The list published by the Department of Finance was so overbroad that it even included my name, and I don't mind my name and my home address, but I've been in that damn home for 365 days a year since 1994.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't leave the city and I don't have a second home.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We want to know today how all of those names ended up on the list and why the Department of Finance published a list of property owners when admittedly

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: they knew that the vast majority of the properties on the list were not in fact used as a pied-à-terre.

chapters.summary: Brewer notes that 17,000 property owners received notices, many of whom are primary residents. She criticizes the burden being on homeowners to prove residency rather than the city verifying existing records like the co-op and condo abatement.
chapters.title: Brewer addresses notification letters and burden of proof on homeowners

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finance ultimately only sent notifications to around 17,000 property owners, notifying them that they would be subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That number is still larger than most estimates.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My office and other council members, we have received calls from constituents who received these letters.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Even though

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The property listed is their primary residence and has been for many years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Homeowners who believe that they received the letters in error initially had only a short window to contest the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Although the deadline was ultimately extended by four weeks, this still puts a burden on property owners, which upset people tremendously.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They have to prove, not the city, that the property in question is their primary residence.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Rather than, as I said, the onus being on the city to ensure that only properties being used as the pied-à-terre are subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The city already has plenty of records showing which taxpayers are city residents.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For example, the co-op and condo abatement already requires that property owners submit documentation

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: showing that the units are owner-occupied, so DOF should already know that these units are not peer-to-peers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: DOF should have used the information they already had before publishing people's names and addresses and requiring them to affirmatively prove again

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that they reside in the city.

chapters.summary: Brewer points out that nearly 42,000 property owners have applied for exemptions, and that DOF is wasting public resources re-collecting documentation it already possesses. She notes the mayor and commissioner acknowledged using outdated records.
chapters.title: Brewer highlights wasted resources and 42,000 exemption applications

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not only does this create a burden for taxpaying New Yorkers, but now finance needs to spend time and resources processing every application for an abatement

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and collecting and verifying documentation that already has collected and verifying, in my opinion,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Wasting public resources.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So far, nearly 42,000

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: property owners have applied for or in the process of applying for an exemption to tax because either they are using the property as their primary residence or because they are eligible for some other exemption.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Both the mayor and finance commissioner Richard Lee, for whom we have great respect,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: have already acknowledged that the records that they were using to identify properties subject to the tax were outdated and that they knew when they posted the initial list that it included a large number of properties that would not be subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think we all want to know why the city published a list that it knew was not accurate.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Like many of my constituents, I have a lot of questions about this tax that we are hoping to get answers to.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I do want to thank the council staff members who made this possible, from Government Operations Committee, Johari Frazier, Erica Cohen, and Sigma Hamid, and from the Finance Committee, Brian Sarfo and Owen Kotowski,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and Cynthia Hornick from my office and everybody else.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks council staff and the Department of Finance for constituent assistance, then turns the floor over to Finance Chair Linda Lee.
chapters.title: Brewer thanks staff and introduces Chair Lee

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I do want to also say I do thank the Department of Finance because they have been helpful for those constituents who need help.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't want people to think that has not happened because it has.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Now I'm going to turn to the wonderful Chair Lee.

chapters.summary: Finance Chair Linda Lee explains the surcharge applies to 1-3 family homes valued at $5M+ and condo/co-op units valued at $1M+ that are not primary residences. She notes DOF mailed 17,000 notices and published a supplemental roll of 900,000+ properties.
chapters.title: Chair Lee explains the pied-à-terre tax framework and rollout scope

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Great, thank you so much, Chair Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Welcome again to today's oversight hearing on the implementation and rollout of the city's pied-a-terre tax, also known as the non-primary residence property surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: The pied-a-terre tax

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: X was enacted as part of the state's fiscal year 2026-27 budget and took effect on July 1, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: The surcharge applies to one to three family homes valued at $5 million or more, as well as condominium and cooperative units valued at $1 million or more that do not serve as the owner's primary residence.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Properties that serve as the primary residence of the owner, an immediate family member, or a qualifying tenant are not subject to the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Since implementation began, Department of Finance has mailed notices to approximately 17,000 property owners identified as potentially subject to the surcharge and has published a supplemental roll listing more than 900,000 properties that may fall within the tax scope.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Given the scale of this rollout and the number of New Yorkers who have been affected, it is crucial that this Council conduct oversight of how the administration is planning on implementing this new tax.

chapters.summary: Lee explains that due to ongoing litigation, the administration is not testifying today. She says the Council will send written questions and looks forward to engagement after litigation resolves. She outlines the hearing's goal of hearing from advocates and affected owners.
chapters.title: Lee addresses administration's absence and litigation concerns

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Following litigation initiated by a group of city homeowners, the administration extended the deadline for property owners to file exemptions from late August to September 18th.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Still, even with the extension, we seek greater guidance for those impacted to ensure that this rollout is smooth.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Given this ongoing litigation, I want to note again for the record that the administration will not be participating in today's hearing, and we understand the sensitivity of testifying while this matter is before the courts, and we look forward to continued engagement

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: with the administration once the litigation is resolved and to providing answers to city homeowners directly impacted by the rollout of the tax.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: In the meantime, today's hearing will afford us an opportunity to hear from advocates, affected property owners, and other stakeholders about the impact of this rollout to date and how to ensure that the Department of Finance's implementation of this surcharge is fair,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: transparent, and legally sound going forward.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: We intend to send the administration written questions for follow-up in response to testimony shared by the public and questions prepared by myself and my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I want to thank all the staff who helped make this hearing possible, especially the Council's Committee on Finance and Committee on Governmental Operations in preparing today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And now I turn it back over to Chair Brewer.

chapters.summary: Brewer announces the hearing format: she will read the Finance Commissioner's written testimony, then hear from the public, and finally read the questions that would have been asked of the administration. She notes council members in attendance.
chapters.title: Brewer explains format: reading DOF testimony, public testimony, and prepared questions

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair Lee.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And what will happen now is I'm going to read the testimony from the Finance Department.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from the constituents, as you heard.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then Chair Lee and I will read the questions that we would have asked, but we will be sending for answers to every single one of them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Council Member Dinowitz is here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And on Zoom, Council Member Felice and Maloney.

chapters.summary: Brewer reads Commissioner Richard Lee's testimony explaining the state legislation authorizing the surcharge, enacted May 2026, and the rulemaking process including a public hearing on July 9 and final rules adopted July 14, 2026.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lee's written testimony: legal framework and rulemaking process

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Dear Gail Brewer, Chair Linda Lee, and members of the City Council, my name is Richard Lee, and I am the Commissioner of New York City Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony regarding the implementation of the surcharge on non-primary resident properties commonly referred to as pied-à-terre.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I understand the Council's interest in holding this hearing to discuss the implementation of this surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The public understandably has a range of questions about this surcharge and the manner in which it has been implemented.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have been engaged with members of your team and directly with many of you, he has, absolutely, to ensure that New Yorkers have the information that they need.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I would have welcomed the opportunity to appear in person and field your questions directly, but the pending and active litigation precludes me from doing so.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The administration requested that the City Council postpone the hearing to the near future, but the Council declined.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In the meantime, I appreciate the opportunity to address some of those questions in my written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: First, let me walk through the steps that led to implementation of the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: From the passage of the state legislation authorizing the surcharge,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: through the rulemaking process to the posting of a supplemental role and transmission of initial determination letters.

chapters.summary: The testimony explains the city's long-standing practice of publishing assessment rolls, the requirement to publish a supplemental mid-cycle roll for the surcharge, and that the data has been publicly available for over a century through various systems including ACRIS.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lee's testimony: assessment roll history and publication requirements

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: On May 28, 2026, as part of State's 2627 budget legislation,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: the state enacted Part HH of Chapter 59 of 2026, which authorized this surcharge on certain high-value New York City residential properties

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that are not used as a primary residence.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The law was enacted with support from the mayor and his administration to help close a significant budget gap.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The statutory provisions relating to this surcharge can be found in Article 30-C of the New York State Tax Law and Chapter 32 of Title 11 of the City's Admin Code.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As with all revenue collected by the Department of Finance, these funds keep help the city running.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The revenue DOF collects supports essential services that New Yorkers rely on every day, from educating our children in public schools and maintaining our parks to ensuring our streets are clean and our trash is collected.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Department of Finance took steps to ensure the surcharge would be implemented through a transparent, consistent, and fair process that is legal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: compliant.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: On June 9, 2026, the Department of Finance published proposed rules outlining how the new surcharge would be administered and applied.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As part of the rulemaking process, property owners and other members of the public had an opportunity to submit written feedback

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: provide testimony, and raise questions or concerns at a public hearing held on July 9, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Department of Finance reviewed the feedback that it received through the notice and comment process, made appropriate adjustments to the rule text, and promulgated the final rules necessary to implement the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: These rules were thereafter adopted on July 14, 2026 and took effect immediately.

chapters.summary: The testimony details the July 2026 supplemental roll publication, explaining that covered property is broader than properties subject to the surcharge. The supplemental roll does not establish which properties are subject to the tax but provides a basis for challenges.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lee's testimony: supplemental roll and covered property universe

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: After adopting these rules, the Department of Finance moved forward with implementing the surcharge and as required by law, published a supplemental role on its website.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Each year, the city publishes real property market values and assessed values for all taxable property through its annual assessment roll.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The purpose of the assessment roll is to provide the public with notice about every property subject to real property taxation throughout the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The assessed and market values associated

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: with such property and certain information necessary to identify the property and its ownership.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Both the real property tax law and the city charter require the city to publish an assessment roll of taxable property in this manner, and assessment rolls have been required to be published annually

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: for well over a century.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In accordance with the city charter, Finance publishes the tentative assessment role for the upcoming fiscal year every January, January 15th to be exact.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Upon publication of this tentative assessment role, property owners may challenge certain assessment related matters

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: including by making a filing with the city's independent tax commission.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: On the date the tax commission is required to render final determinations on these challenges, May 25 of each year, Finance releases its final assessment roll.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The city's assessment role is highly accessible to the public and it has been for many years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Any suggestion to the contrary is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For example, this property data has been publicly available as a fully searchable database on both the finance website

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and New York City Open Data.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finances online archives include a

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: assessment roll data dating back to fiscal year 2009.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Many data elements included on the roll relating to property ownership are culled from land records and have also been available

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: through the Department of Finance's automated city register information system known to all of us as ACRES.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The city has published assessment rolls and made them available for public examination in various forms for over 100 years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Before internet accessibility, the city's assessment rolls and land records were made available for review in person at government offices.

chapters.summary: The testimony explains that only 17,000 of 960,000 listed properties received initial determination letters. Properties with existing primary residency proof, such as SCHE/DHE recipients, were excluded. The letters are not tax bills but allow owners to submit proof of primary residency.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lee's testimony: initial determination letters and exemption process

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Section 11-3205 of the Admin Code, part of the statutory framework,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: governing the surcharge, requires the city to administer and enforce the surcharge, quote, to the greatest extent practicable,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: in the same manner used to administer and enforce real property taxes, unquote, and requires the publication of corresponding property valuation information

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: on a roll.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The law authorizing the surcharge was adopted after the assessment roll for fiscal year 2627 had already been published.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As a result, the law governing the surcharge required the city to release a supplemental mid-cycle roll

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: for the 2627 tax year in order for the

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: surcharge to be administered.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Stated differently, for the 26-27 fiscal year only, Finance published a new assessment role mid-year, the July 2026 supplemental role.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This largely involved republishing data from the May 2-6 final assessment role.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finance published the required supplemental role on July 24, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This supplemental role includes relevant property valuation information and certain descriptive information regarding all property.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That meets the surcharge statute definition of quote, covered property, unquote.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The universe of the properties considered covered property for purposes of the law is much broader than the properties that were sent initial determination letters

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: as explained below or that will eventually be subject to the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In light of this, it is important to emphasize what the supplemental rule does not do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The supplemental rule does not establish which properties are subject to the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It generally includes certain information to identify such properties and their ownership.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Like the assessment roll, publication of the supplemental roll provides a basis for property owners to change.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: challenge the value of their properties.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The law also requires finance to send initial determination letters to property owners whose properties may be subject to the surcharge

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and whose primary residency could not be confirmed based on the information available to the agency as described in finance rules.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Only a very small subset of the population of properties that were listed in the supplemental roll

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: received an initial determination letter, about 17,000 homes out of approximate total of 960,000 listed homes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The surcharge only applies to those Class 1 properties, which typically include one to three family homes, with market values greater than or equal to $5 million,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and cooperative and condominium dwelling units with market values greater than or equal to $1 million.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Some properties that would have otherwise received an initial determination letter did not ultimately receive one because finance already possessed data

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that sufficiently demonstrated that the property was used as a primary residence and was therefore not subject to the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For example,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Homeowners who affirmatively established primary residency with finance already were the two

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 627 fiscal year, such as homeowners who received the Senior Citizens Homeowners Exemption, known as SHI,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: or the Disabled Homeowners Exemption, known as D, and therefore have provided proof of residency as well as proof of income for eligibility, did not receive this initial determination letter.

chapters.summary: The testimony describes DOF's outreach efforts through senior centers, community meetings, a dedicated website, 311, and partnerships with elected officials. The deadline for appeals was extended to September 18, 2026. Lee expresses willingness to testify after August 31.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lee's testimony: outreach, customer service, and deadline extension

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One of the most important aspects of this procedure is that this initial determination is not a tax bill.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: These notices simply inform property owners that, based on the information currently available to finance, their property may be subject to the new surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This is an initial determination, not a final one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Property owners who believe their property should not be subject to the surcharge

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: have an opportunity to submit proof the property is used as the primary residence.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This process allows property owners to provide information that is readily available to the owners, but may not be reflected in finance's records.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Through this process, property owners can provide Department of Finance with the information finance needs to make accurate determination regarding surcharge eligibility before the surcharge is applied.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For example,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A primary homeowner can submit their dry

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: driver's license as proof of primary resident.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Property owners can alternatively challenge finances initial determination directly with the tax commission if they are also challenging their market value.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For 2627 tax year,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They have until March 2027 to do so.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In implementing the surcharge, we have focused on providing transparency about which properties may be affected and ensuring homeowners have a straightforward way to resolve their status.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We recognize that homeowners need clear information

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and meaningful support as they navigate the process.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That is why the Department of Finance has prioritized direct assistance and outreach.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finance has been engaging homeowners and plans to further conduct proactive outreach at senior centers, community meetings, and other public forums.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Provide information through our dedicated website, nyc.gov slash npsearcharch and 311.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And continue to work with co-op and condominium boards, property managers, and building representatives to share information with residents.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where contact information for a property owner is available.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We are also reaching out directly to homeowners who receive notices to answer questions and

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: provide guidance on the initial determination appeals process.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In addition, we are partnering with elected officials, community leaders, and constituent services staff to distribute accurate information and connect homeowners with available resources.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We've also announced an extension through September 18th, 2026 for homeowners to submit appeals of initial determinations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We believe these efforts reflect the administration's commitment to ensure that every potentially affected homeowner understands the process, knows where to turn for support,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and has a fair opportunity to challenge a finance initial determination.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I understand there are concerns regarding this surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I also understand that there are individuals who received an initial determination letter who may not ultimately owe the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That is exactly why the Finance Department has expanded its customer service and extended the deadline for property owners to challenge initial determinations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finance is working directly with building managers, elected officials, and homeowners to answer questions and make the process as straightforward as possible.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Whenever government implements a new law affecting thousands of property owners, questions inevitably arise.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Government should communicate clearly and effectively

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: about new policies, and finance is committed to doing that, not just with respect to this law, but of course all aspects of finance's work.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Department of Finance is committed to ensuring that this surcharge is only applied to those properties that are subject to the surcharge under the law.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finance is focused on making sure every homeowner has the information they need to understand the key contours of the law and determine whether they are subject to the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Finance's role is to administer and implement the law.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As implementation moves forward, finance has continued to engage with elected officials

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: respond to constituent concerns, and provide updates and guidance to help New Yorkers navigate the process.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We welcome continued feedback from the City Council and all stakeholders as we work to administer this new law with fairness, consistency, and clarity.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I am prepared and welcome the opportunity to testify after August 31.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That concludes from the Commissioner.

chapters.summary: Kyle Bragg supports taxing the wealthy but raises concerns about the rollout's lack of clarity. He shares a story of a retired friend who bought a brownstone 40 years ago, now worth over $5 million, who is worried about being subject to the tax despite living in the city.
chapters.title: Kyle Bragg testifies on confusion and unintended consequences for everyday New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: Good afternoon, esteemed council members and fellow New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: My name is Kyle Bragg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: I want to be clear that any legislation that's proposed to hold the wealthy accountable to their fair share is a good thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: My challenge is the rollout and how unclear and leaves so many questions in the minds of so many hardworking New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: By way of example, I had a friend call me just recently asking me to explain whether or not he believes he might be subject to the Peter Tare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: He's worked over 50 years in this city, he and his wife.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: Bought a brownstone 40 years ago at near $400,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: Now he believes it's worth over $5 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: He's retired to the South to seek warmer weather and to stretch his retirement dollars out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: And he's concerned now because he kept his brownstone here so they can feed him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: with his kids and his grandkids, whether or not he'd be subject to the Peter Tear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: It's the unknown factor and unknown intent or consequences to the Peter Tear that is troubling to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: It's not only billionaires that are concerned, it's the everyday hardworking New Yorkers who've dedicated themselves to making this city work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: That are very concerned about what impact it might have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: And my challenge is, as well as all the people I've spoken to, is what does it mean to them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: Is there any unknown consequences or impact to hardworking New Yorkers who this was not intended to affect?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: So thank you for your time and thank you for allowing me to speak.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, next.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Jason, go ahead.

chapters.summary: Jason Haber of the American Real Estate Association criticizes the publication of 959,710 names and addresses as a gift to fraudsters. He argues the list creates practical obscurity concerns and questions why the burden is on individuals rather than government.
chapters.title: Jason Haber testifies on data privacy risks of the 900,000-property list

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: My name is Jason Haber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: I'm the co-founder of the American Real Estate Association and the president of NYRAC, the leading real estate voice here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: I've also been a licensed real estate broker for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: First, a thank you to the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: You know, when the state legislature first proposed this tax in the first place, there was no hearing on the tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And so today is actually citizens'first opportunity to speak to a legislative body about the tax, and in today's case, in its execution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: So thank you for that, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Let's begin with the obvious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Let's begin with the docs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: The city published 959,710 names and addresses on a downloadable spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: With two clicks, a person could download an entire list larger than the population of San Francisco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Imagine the gift that this is to fraudsters, to scammers, to anyone with ill will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Now, what does the administration have to say about the release of this information?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Well, we heard from the letter that they're not able to comment today yet in 2016 during pending litigation, in 2017 during pending litigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: They appeared before this council, yet not today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: They will tell you, though, that this information was already public, but there is a difference between public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: and published.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Any one of these records could be pulled from ACRIS, but to pull 959,710 records would take a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: single person working eight hours a day, five days a week, 15 years, or roughly 498 scaramuchis, depending on how you mark time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Now the courts have a name for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: They call it practical obscurity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: The Supreme Court principle that information no one can feasibly assemble is functionally private.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: That obscurity was willfully erased by the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: The Department of Finance did 15 years of labor for anyone who wished these New Yorkers harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: They handed it out, sorted it, and searchable for free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And what did this list have to do with the tax in the first place?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: According to officials, the pool of taxed homes is around 13,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: So how did that swell 74 times?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And why is the burden on the individual instead of on the enormity of government?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Why is it guilty until proven resident?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer herself was on the list, as she said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Although, to be fair, Councilmember Brewer is at 10 events a night and sometimes in two places at once.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: So perhaps for her, it is a pied-a-terre since she's never there and always out in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Look, I'm not here to litigate the tax itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: That debate is not with this body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: But I'm here to talk about the execution and when that execution fails its citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Was this a dox by accident, by incompetence, or hubris?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Keep asking questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: The citizens of New York deserve better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: They deserve to know why this happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Quiet, quiet, quiet, quiet, quiet.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead, next.

chapters.summary: Mary Ann Rothman of the Council of NY Cooperatives and Condominiums explains that the law makes co-ops responsible for collecting and remitting the surcharge, a major departure from past practice. She urges DOF to collect directly from non-resident shareholders instead.
chapters.title: Mary Ann Rothman testifies on co-op collection burden and direct payment proposal

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Lee and Chair Brewer, and thank you for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: My name's Mary Ann Rothman, and I'm the Executive Director of the Council of New York Cooperatives and Condominiums, a not-for-profit membership organization that's been providing information, education, and advocacy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: to and for housing cooperatives and condominiums since 1975.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: The state legislation that created the Pietater tax surcharge made cooperatives responsible for collecting and remitting to the Department of Finance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: the surcharge due from shareholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: This is a huge departure from past practices where DOF has provided documentation to enable cooperatives to distribute credit to shareholders who qualify for exemptions and abatements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Never before have cooperatives had to collect funds and remit them to DOF.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Any cooperative unable to collect from a shareholder in time for the January 1st, 2027 payment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: will need to invade reserves or assess shareholders or borrow funds to keep the building's property taxes current.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: The smaller the building, the larger the portion of the non-residents owners'piet a terre tax that each resident shareholder will have to find a way to pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Where is the justice in jeopardizing the financial stability of a cooperative in this way?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Instead, the Department of Finance should collect the Pieta Terre tax directly from each affected non-resident shareholder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: DOF is already in communication with them by letter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: And there's the precedent, parking tickets, et cetera, for the department to collect payment directly from individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Our organization is seeking Senate and Assembly sponsors for legislation to amend the Pieta-Ter tax to have the surcharge remitted directly to the Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: We hope that the City Council will support this practical and reasonable goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: Oh, you pushed that, okay.

chapters.summary: Thor Thors, a co-op owner, shares that his entire building was listed because one penthouse unit exceeded the value threshold. He describes the list as an invasion of privacy and characterizes the rollout as reflecting socialist policies by the administration.
chapters.title: Thor Thors testifies on privacy concerns and building-wide list exposure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Tor Tors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: I'm a lifelong New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: I'm not speaking on behalf of any organization, simply myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: I am a co-op owner here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And I just want to share what the rollout of this tax meant to me personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: If any of you live in co-ops, you know that when you get assessments, as this woman said, we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: It can be very disruptive to your economic situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And that goes for all different types of co-op owners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: Most of the co-ops in my building do not fall in the range of over a million dollars as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: judged by the finance department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: However, there is one that does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: It's a penthouse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: It's three combined apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: So I believe as a result of that one penthouse being, our whole building was on the list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And I was able to personally download and see

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: the alleged value of everybody's apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And, you know, what it really feels to me like is it's the administration or the powers that be saying, we see you, you know, we see the value of the apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: We're willing to expose you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: We're willing to tell everyone how much your apartment is worth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And I believe it's a direct result of the policies of this administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: I think they've said as much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: I'm not really asking questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: That's what I believe that it comes from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: Socialist policies from a socialist administration that is manifested in the rollout of this very unfortunate doxing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Rebecca Poole of CNYC highlights that co-ops are not set up to collect surcharges, the $1M imputed market value doesn't equate to $5M sales price, and raises concerns about retroactive application affecting longtime homeowners who now owe $80,000.
chapters.title: Rebecca Poole testifies on co-op affordability, valuation issues, and retroactive concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the Committees on Finance and Governmental Operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: My name is Rebecca Poole, and I'm the Director of Membership and Communication for the Council of New York Cooperatives and Condominiums.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: CMYC's membership includes over 100,000 co-op and condo homeowners

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: across all generations living in member buildings ranging in size from two apartments to well over 6,000 units in 47 of the 51 council districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: As outlined in CMYC's recently released report on co-op and condo affordability issues,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: co-op and condo homeowners are struggling with escalating housing costs and well understand the city's need to close the budget gap without further increasing expenses for the majority of New York City's homeowners and residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Therefore, CMYC does not oppose a surcharge on luxury second homes that have sold for more than $5 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: CMYC appreciates the difficulty in implementing this type of surcharge and believes that several changes to the state legislation would help resolve the strain that the surcharge will place on New York City homeowners, particularly in co-ops and condos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: We have attached our comments on the state legislation and rules, but I will highlight three key issues that concern us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Co-ops and condos, as Mary Ann mentioned, are not set up to collect these substantial sums, such as a PAT surcharge, from individual shareholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: and the requirement that the co-op take on this responsibility could be devastating, particularly to a small co-op where the PAT charge may be larger than the entire co-op's real estate taxes for the year in a four- or five-unit co-op.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: The $1 million imputed market value of the co-op or condo as used in the legislation does not equate to $5 million sales price or market value, particularly in Class 2C co-ops and condos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Our analysis of Class 2C condominiums that sold between 2021 and 2026 show that 68% of these apartments with an imputed market value of $1 million

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: actually sold for less than $5 million in the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: There are issues with the definition and proof of primary residency, who qualifies as family members, and what happens upon the sale and or alteration of an apartment, or the death of the existing shareholder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: CMYC's recommendations regarding these issues are clearly laid out in our comments on the rules in state legislation, which you'll be provided with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Lastly, I'd like to add that our concern over the retroactive nature of this surcharge,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: what it did was remove options from some longtime homeowners who have resided in New York City for over 40 years and purchased their home in the 1970s,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: and now found out that because they were not primary residents on January 5th of 2026, already passed, they owe $80,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: We welcome the opportunity to work with the Council, the MAMDONI administration, and state legislature in ensuring there's a solution that works for all parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to say that Councilmember Arola is on Zoom and Brooks Powers is here with us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: People may have questions for this panel.
