utterances.text: Because I'm hearing that.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Do any of you have a concern of people knowing where you're at and how much approximately your house worth?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And especially we have so many scammers around as we always, you know, been fighting against.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So anyone can answer that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: I would just say that it's just been totally confusing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: There's no conversation that I've had with anyone in this city that really understands the Peter Day attacks and the impact on them personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: And I'm talking about people who've lived and worked in this city their entire lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: And so there's lack of clarity, and that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: That's a problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: You're rolling out such an important piece of legislation, and people don't understand whether or not it has an impact on them personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: People, we're not talking about the wealthy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: We're not talking about billionaires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: We're talking about everyday New Yorkers who spent their entire lives in service to making this city better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: So, hey, I think there's, you know, the lack of clarity, lack of information that's available to people around the rollout of the Peter T.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kyle Bragg
utterances.text: Tax is a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Councilman, if I could just address that also, I think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: A foreign actor has already downloaded that list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: and can very easily do a mailing, make it look like it's from a city official, and say something like, pay $50 or $100, and so you won't be subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: There are plenty of seniors, unfortunately, who already know all too well that they can be victims of scams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: This is a perfect opportunity for those with bad intent to reach out to seniors on that list and target them for fraud.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And on the letter you receive or your friend receive, do they give them an opportunity to appeal if they need to?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Any option that you have, like they have?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Do they get any?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I mean, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: But I think the process is that the burden is on that person, not on the government itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And I think that they have that inverted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And so they've put people, again, seniors in an awkward position.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: You know how hard it can be just to having a senior upload information to their social security account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And now we're asking them to do something they've never done before and or hire an attorney to do it, which adds an additional cost and burden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: The burden is reversed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: It should be on the city, not on the citizen.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I got you.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: The co-op, I'm still having a little problem with that because I know I'm dealing with a lot of folks.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And like you said, some of the condo, they may worth whatever they are mine.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And in the long run, you cannot even sell it for probably three quarter of the price if you're lucky.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: The surcharge, I'm wondering how the board is taking it.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Is the board dealing with that and how they help the folks?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And most of you are probably seniors in the condo or co-op.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So in your case, do they give opportunity to discuss how we're going to face the challenges of the surcharge?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Rebecca, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: So a lot of boards and property managers have been providing education and holding meetings with their shareholders and union owners to explain the tax and the rollout.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: The concern is really...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: For a co-op is what happens if the PIA-TER is actually a PIA-TER and the shareholder doesn't pay the $40,000 or $80,000, then the rest of the building would need to make up that amount.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: So in a 10-unit building, if the charge is $80,000, you know, all the other shareholders are kicking up slightly less than $8,000 each, right, in order to pay

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: that portion of their real estate taxes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: So that's the primary concern for co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: So thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: And pied-à-terre, if we get the meaning of it, is just a little laying on the ground to have a little.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: But now we're going to have to redefine what pied-à-terre is.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member David Carr criticizes the list publication as unprecedented and the burden of proof as inverted. He asks the panel whether the rollout was effective and for comments on DOF's property valuation system. Haber calls it 'botched' and describes easily manipulating the downloaded data.
chapters.title: CM Carr questions panel on rollout effectiveness and DOF valuation system

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Council Member Zouang.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is also here, and we want to hear a question from Councilmember Carr.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, particularly for presiding over this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's crucially important.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I'm just here on behalf of the many of the over 900,000 folks who are on that list

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: inappropriately because so many constituents are in fear and in confusion at a minimum based on the release of their information in a way that's unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Everybody in government knows for years the city publishes its tax rolls, but never has it been so easy to get at that information and to give a roadmap.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: To individual property owners across the city, many of whom it's the biggest investment they ever made or the biggest investment their family ever made.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And to be made to appear to be victims because of their success as a family, which is why so many of us came here over the generations, is a shame.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And despite what was said in the testimony from the finance department, I do not believe a plain text reading of the law

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: meant that they needed to publish this list in this way.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: They only needed to send out determination letters to those they believe were subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I couldn't agree more with what was said.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It is a total inversion of the burden of proof for the city to be the ones telling property owners, it's on you to prove that you're actually a resident here.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's on you to prove that you lease or rent out your property to a residential tenant.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I really want to commend Speaker Menon and the leadership here of the two committees for trying to make sure that this rollout never gets bungled again, because that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And in particular, I'm disappointed that we can't ask the Finance Department directly in a hearing today any questions at all, but in particular, another issue that hasn't gotten enough attention, which is, are the Finance Department's evaluations of properties correct?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: There are many in this room and on this dais who spent years wading into that debate.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Nobody thinks the finance department's evaluations are correct.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's a systemic problem that's been wrong for decades.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And now we're relying on that flawed system to determine whether or not certain properties should be subject to the pied-a-terre tax.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And in particular, so many of my neighbors, none of whom...

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: None of whom meet the property threshold, the financial threshold, to be included on any list with respect to a second home tax.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It just beggars belief that this is where we're at today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So my question to the panel, whomever wished to ask, is do you believe that this rollout was done effectively or appropriately?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And secondarily, what are your comments on the Department of Finance's evaluation system in a general sense or with particularity to condos, co-ops, or one- and two-, three-family homes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Councilman, the only word to use is botch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: It was botched.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And just to further your point, Councilman, the weekend that the list was downloadable, I downloaded it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: I downloaded it, I created an app in two hours, I was able to sort it using API information also about age, and I could integrate age integration in if I wanted to create a targeted list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And I decided not to release it, I kept it locally on my computer because I thought someone could use it with malintent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: If I could do it in two hours and I'm not even a computer programmer, imagine what someone could do who wanted to do harm to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: It's just that easy and it's just wrong.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong next.

chapters.summary: Council Member Phil Wong criticizes the administration's absence and the burden on residents to prove residency. He asks panelists if they feel safe with the list public. Thors expresses concern about the administration putting homeowners 'on the hot seat.'
chapters.title: CM Wong questions panel on safety risks and administration transparency

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So much for transparency.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The administration is refusing to send anyone to answer questions for a rollout that has already produced thousands of challenges, widespread confusion,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: a court fight, and nearly 2,700 homeowners who have been told the city got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And the Charter Revision Commission already showed that the mayor's view of the council's checks and balances are not something this administration respects when they get in the way.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, at the hearing convened to conduct oversight of the mayor's own tax rollout, the administration is sending no one.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I would like to say this.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My residents in my district shouldn't have to hire lawyers to prove they live in their own home.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And if the city can pull tax data, the statute allows finance to pull tax data to verify residency, it makes no sense that the work is being handed to the homeowner to do that instead.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question is, do you feel safe now that the list is out there?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or you think we'll all be targets of fraud, threats, harassments?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Anyone answer that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Somebody besides Jason.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I love Jason, but somebody besides Jason can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: I'm more concerned, rather than specific safety, I'm more concerned that this administration is putting homeowners on the hot seat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: That what they're saying is, we know how much, we know who you are, we know how much your apartment is worth, it's all up in the air now, there's going to be future taxes, we're going to tax you in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

chapters.summary: Council Member Kamillah Hanks calls the list a 'hit list' and 'scarlet letter,' and asks about properties held in trust. Rebecca Poole explains DOF rules require trust beneficiaries to prove primary residency, though trusts are automatically assumed non-primary.
chapters.title: CM Hanks questions panel on trusts and privacy invasion concerns

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Council Member Hanks?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Brewer, Chair Lee, for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And I just really want to reiterate for the record my earlier statement from before that we really aren't here to dispute the peditaire tax.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: This hearing is about everyday New Yorkers that who, you know, have just been treated in a manner in which

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: is completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And if the administration would have shown the care it took to provide the written testimony, as it did with this botched rollout, we may not be here today answering and asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: The one thing I've learned in my short time having the privilege of representing District 49 in the North Shore of Staten Island,

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: is that how you provide information to your constituents really reflects how you feel about them.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: It reflects respect, because if you respect the people that you represent and you take great care in how that information is provided and absolutely how it's perceived,

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So how the administration published more than 900,000 names and addresses showed me that this is how the administration feels about homeowners in this great city.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: That this is something that we need to be ashamed of.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: A hit list of the haves and the have-nots.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: A scarlet letter.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Letting everyone

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: know, as you had so poignantly said, we know who you are and we see you.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And more importantly, the absence and the written testimony is an amplification of that message.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So my question is,

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Many of my constituents have asked, they found themselves on this larger hit list, but their home is in trust.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And, you know, many people will do estate planning without letting their partners know, their families know.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So this is also like an invasion of privacy on things that are very intimate and how you're going to handle your parents, you know, situations as they get older.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: People put housing in trust.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Can anybody kind of talk to me today about...

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: How that's interpreted when it comes to this kind of list, because that's really the question.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I should be asking the administration, but this is the question that I would say that 10 or more of my constituents have asked, that they are living in their primary home, but it's in a trust.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So I don't know if you have any.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: The Department of Finance rules outline how a beneficiary of a trust can go about proving primary residency, where you provide,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact details, but if you look at the Department of Finance rules, it tells you what information the trust would have to provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the trust is automatically

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: assumed not to be a primary residence, although, you know, perhaps the tax returns of the primary beneficiary could be used to show that that's their address.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I really appreciate you answering my question, but it is not the obligation of this panel to answer these questions, so I hope I didn't put anybody on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: It was kind of rhetorical, but thank you all so much and everybody here that is here in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, and good luck if his in-laws in there, because they're not on the list, just in case you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Council Member Jay Sanchez.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano calls the administration's absence outrageous, arguing litigation doesn't suspend oversight. He questions the discrepancy between the 900,000-property list and 17,000 notices, and asks about error rates and the burden placed on seniors.
chapters.title: CM Morano criticizes administration absence and questions rollout competence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Councilman Morano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Bruin.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Lee, for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you to the public, the members of the public that signed up to testify both here and on Zoom, not only the five of you who we've already heard from who all did a brilliant job, but for everybody to

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: take the time to make sure this doesn't turn into a Clint Eastwood speech of us talking to an empty chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I do want to begin by talking about who's not here today, which obviously is the administration.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And quite frankly, I find that outrageous.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The city was able to identify nearly a million properties and put them on a list connected to this tax.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It was able to find 17,000 homeowners and send them letters telling them they could be subject to a substantial surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But somehow today, the administration couldn't find its way within the same building to City Hall to answer questions about it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I find that to be totally unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They've cited ongoing litigation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, litigation doesn't suspend legislative oversight.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There are plenty of questions about administration, customer service, data, staffing, and basic competence that don't require anybody to discuss litigation strategy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: City administrations testify before this council all...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: the time while litigation is pending.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Jason cited a few examples.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In fact, the law department itself has appeared before the council and discussed active lawsuits involving the city.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just last November, Corporation Council testified about the city's ongoing federal litigation over sanctuary city laws, and the law department routinely

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: appears before this council while simultaneously representing the city in scores, if not hundreds, of active cases.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Nobody is asking the Department of Finance to waive attorney-client privilege or reveal its litigation strategy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're asking basic questions about how a major tax was administered.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What records did you use?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How did you identify the 17,000 homeowners?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many were identified incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why weren't government records cross-checked first?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And why did you publish a supplemental role containing more than 900,000 properties and associate it with the surcharge?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: These are oversight questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So when the administration refuses to sit here and answer them, I think New Yorkers are entitled to ask a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What are they hiding?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I particularly want to address something in the administration's written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They claim they were required to publish this massive supplemental role.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That is very much disputed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The state law as minority leader car sign.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: says the Department of Finance must make an individualized initial determination about whether a covered property is not a primary residence.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What I don't see in that statute is a direction from Albany saying, publish the names and property information of more than 900,000 New Yorkers and describe that list as related to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In fact, the city's own website now acknowledges that the vast majority of the properties on that roll will not be subject to the surcharge.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Only roughly 17,000 owners even receive notices.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So it would have liked the commissioner sitting here today to explain that discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you truly believe state law required this particular list, come before the council, point us to the language, and answer questions about it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But you can't make a sweeping assertion in written testimony, decline to appear, and then expect the council to simply accept it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's precisely why oversight hearings exist.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Litigation is not a hall pass from legislative oversight.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The more New Yorkers and the more this council learned about this whole process, the more clear it was how rotten it was, how bungled it was, and the more questions we had.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I sincerely hope that the administration does not decide to make this routine.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What was the error rate?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We don't know.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We don't want to hear a press release from the administration or a talking point.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We want to hear your error rate.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many New Yorkers did government unnecessarily frighten?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many hours did people collectively spend fixing something that City Hall could have gotten right beforehand?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many seniors had to find documents?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many people called an attorney?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many people simply assumed that because an official letter came from the Department of Finance, they must have done something wrong?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd also ask this, not of you, but of the administration.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The controller estimated that roughly 13,000 properties would be subject to this.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why the difference in that number?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Eric Dinowitz asks about costs co-ops may face including proprietary lease amendments, attorney fees, and insurance problems. Rothman details potential legal and financial consequences, while Thors notes co-op boards may ban pied-à-terres entirely, impacting market prices.
chapters.title: CM Dinowitz questions panel on co-op compliance costs and legal fees

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Dinowitz?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do have to agree, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, we were promised a new era of transparency in this

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: administration and it is deeply disappointing that regardless of whatever is going on in the administration,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: they should show up and answer basic questions about the rollout, the rollout that's clearly impacting tens of thousands of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have a question about co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have a number of co-ops in my district, as you all know.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have a lot of things like local laws, and a lot of local laws, like the Pita-Ter tax, most people support.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Most people support raising money for our city services from non-New Yorkers who have the vacation home in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But like so many of our local laws that deal with the environment or health and safety, there are often costs associated with it, unintended consequences, unintended costs, and quality of life concerns.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because of the amount of work we need to do to comply with these laws.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm wondering, for those of you representing co-ops or living in a co-op, if you not only anticipate

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: concerns about those one or two apartments in the building, but any costs that the building itself may have to pay for those consultants that you're so used to paying for, or legal fees.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Have you paid any of those costs yet, or do you anticipate, as this gets rolled out, that you will be enduring those sorts of costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: So there has already been discussion amongst co-ops about potentially changing proprietary leases in order to deal with the collection of this tax, which won't be done based on a share distribution, but will rather be just assigned to an individual.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: So that's a change on how expenses are usually collected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: So there may be proprietary lease amendments, which will require an attorney.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: And then obviously, if there's a pay a tear and the tax doesn't get paid, there will be an attorney to try to collect the funds to pay to the Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: If the building can't pay the PAA tax and it's left as an expense, there's a potential for insurance problems if the building has to renew their insurance and they have this debt to the city because they haven't been able to collect it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Same thing with if a mortgage renews.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Those are sort of the issues that we've already, you know, people are already planning to try to address depending on how it's rolled out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: And we just wish that there had been some discussion in advance of the legislation being introduced in the state with co-op and condo professionals so that they could have weighed in on these issues before the legislation went through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: If I may add, having served on the board of my co-op, I can tell you that co-op boards are highly risk-averse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: So any little hint that this could cause a problem in the building with assessments or the management of the building

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: will immediately trigger most co-op boards to say, well, we're not going to allow any more pied-à-terre.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: That's just going to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And that's going to close out a large portion of the market in many of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: They're just not going to allow pied-à-terre.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: So that's going to close out a lot of people who may not even be anywhere near the limit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: But they're just going to shut out anybody who's out of town.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: And that's going to severely impact the market, and it's also going to reduce the price of co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thor Thors
utterances.text: They're not going to be able to get the prices that they want.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It seems, so it seems that there are going to, there are costs and concerns associated with this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A tax that I support, by the way, and I think most people in the council support, but without the administration here to even discuss these things on the record in public, it's very difficult to address these issues in a public form.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what the city could do to put the burden on government rather than individual shareholders. Poole says state legislation needs amendment, and Haber suggests taking the list offline and inverting the process so government must demonstrate tax liability.
chapters.title: CM Dinowitz asks panel about city steps to shift burden from co-op shareholders

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So beyond state legislation, which you've mentioned, what steps could the city take?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think the burden should be on the government, not on the individual shareholder or homeowner to address the costs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And in particular, in the case of co-ops, it should certainly not be in the burden should not be on individual shareholders who aren't wouldn't otherwise be subject to this tax.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So what steps should the city be taking to the city government be taking to put the burden on them regarding co-ops?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can we have the mic on, please?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: The state legislation sets up the chart of evaluations and it sets up the process as it is now

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: where the Department of Finance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: can bill the, can have the co-op be the collector for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: So I think we have to work very hard to amend, for amendments to the state law as soon as the state legislature reconvenes, or the new legislature convenes in January.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't think of specifics that we could do here

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: without the right state legislation to help with the implementation of this difficult law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: I would just add that I would invert, if I had a magic wand, I would get the list off the internet immediately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: I would invert the whole process and allow for the enormity of government to be required to tax the citizens and demonstrate it not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: I think those basic steps would cure a lot of confusion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And would be fair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Haber
utterances.text: And I think that's a step in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Vickie Paladino calls the administration's absence a 'disgrace' and characterizes the tax as a form of eminent domain designed to force property foreclosures. She urges the list be taken down immediately and criticizes the burden of proof being on citizens.
chapters.title: CM Paladino criticizes administration absence and calls tax 'eminent domain'

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Paul Adino on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody, and thank you very much for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And to the two chairs, thank you for hosting this very, very important and troubling hearing to echo what has been said again and again by my colleagues Carr and Morano.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It's an absolute disgrace that the administration is not here to address these people, let alone us.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is extremely, extremely troubling.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This list is indeed a targeted list.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Let's cut to the chase here.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: When you tax people to the point of, let's say, that's one woman who spoke about a family that bought their house in 1970,

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: was not aware, of course, that there was going, and they bought a second home in Florida or wherever, that they're going to be facing something like $40,000 or more in back taxes or the new tax that's being implemented.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This tax is being implemented for one reason.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It's being implemented because we've watched this administration go after private ownership.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We've watched this happen continuously.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It's been on his agenda since he ran for office.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So our mayor and the people who surround our mayor and the state government.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is eminent domain, folks, because if you cannot pay your property taxes, what happens after that?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They come in and they swoop up.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is one of the ways in which they can foreclose on a property, be it a co-op and condo or be a private home ownership.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This has been the ultimate goal of this administration from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And the fact that they are not here, to Frank's point, leaning on their legal...

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Troubles that they're having or what's happening in court.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: That is not reason to be here.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They are not there because they do not want to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is considered a foregone conclusion.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And this is a shame that these nice people, regular New Yorkers, came out.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: To talk to what they hope and get answers to what they hope would be the confusion.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And there are 900,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: How is this possible?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: There's so many question marks to this.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is a targeted list.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And to everybody on that panel, you made a perfect...

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Perfect statement, each and every one of you.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: But I want the people of the city of New York who can hear us today, and this will be recorded, I highly advise you to watch very carefully because the burden of proof is being left to the individual citizen.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Once again, it's being left to the individual citizen.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They will have to bear the burden of proof.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is totally unfair and coward and absolute cowardness of this administration.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Because they watch everything that goes on.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And yes, I'm being very critical of Zoran Mondani and his entire housing czar and their whole committee that they set up.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is all part of a plan.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is ultimate eminent domain.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Who is going to be able to pay $40,000, $80,000 in back taxes and then pay lawyers to go up against the finance department and drag their cases into court?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And to the other gentleman's point with real estate, take that list down immediately.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Immediately take that list down.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is so unfair and cowardness, cowardness on our mayor.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving me the time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Charles Diamond, a former city employee, criticizes the release of personally identifiable information for over 98% of people not subject to the tax. He calls the administration's refusal to testify 'unacceptable' and urges the council to condemn the action.
chapters.title: Charles Diamond testifies on PII release concerns and administration absence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I'll begin, Chair, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Lee, Chair Brewer, the entire council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: My name is Charles Diamond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I worked for the city for nearly a decade, including probably close to a dozen implementations of state law changes into local law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I'm here today to speak in my personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I don't even own a home, but I'm so disturbed by this process that I felt the need to kind of point out what I saw and to really thank the council for refusing to abridge its responsibilities during a time like this and holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Regardless of one's thoughts on the underlying policy, the release of personally identifying information by the city, like names and addresses, is usually a torturous process on purpose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Talk about all of the different times when we released PII, and there are reasons why this takes a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: In this case, over 98% of the PII that was released are of people who are palpably not subject to that tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That kind of over-inclusion of PII should be extremely concerning to us all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: If it was in furtherance of a PR objective, that should be even more concerning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I found it very disturbing, the argument of the finance commissioner in his written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: that this information is otherwise publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's not usually the standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: When the government collates and releases and publishes information in a different way, it carries its own risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Chair, you and I have spoken about this in a previous time with procurement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Talk about the cautions list, a list of people who have gotten poor performance reviews.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The city has refused to ever publish one list like that because of the use of the phrase I think someone else used, it would be a scarlet letter and could be used in negative ways and give a negative implication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's about contractors who choose to contract with the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Yet for some reason that normal analysis, that normal cautious analysis didn't happen here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: And we need to ask why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So thank you for doing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: What is even more disturbing and more important is the fact that no one from the administration is here to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It is unacceptable to use the idea of pending litigation as a reason not to testify in an oversight hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Almost every city action is subject to some potential litigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: I myself have sat here during the asylum response hearings and there have been individual questions when I said, you know what, I cannot answer that question due to litigation or pending actions, but here's what I can talk about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Here's how it generally works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: That's how it's supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: In fact, what this really reminds me of is an incident in the last administration when the Director of Intergovernmental Affairs read their testimony in, stood up and walked out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: The entire council at that time was unanimous in their condemnation of the administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: In this instance, they didn't even show up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It was bizarre, Chair, to hear you read in a commissioner's testimony into the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: It is utterly...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: Utterly bizarre.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So in that sense, I urge the council to condemn the actions of the administration in this instance, when it may be less politically convenient, because they've shown through their actions that they do not consider the council as an equal

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: partner in government, contrary to many of their assertions before getting here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Diamond
utterances.text: So thank you to the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Anna Champaney of the Citizens Budget Commission outlines implementation problems including limited vetting, compressed timeline, and insufficient communications. CBC does not support the tax but emphasizes quality tax administration and recommends evaluating the tax's impact on property values and revenues.
chapters.title: Anna Champaney testifies on implementation challenges and CBC recommendations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: I'm Anna Champany, the Vice President for Research at the Citizens Budget Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Clearly, implementation thus far has been rocky.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Insufficient vetting, compressed rollout, and inadequate communications all contributed to confusion, and both the city and the state can learn from the early stumbles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: CBC does not support the pied-a-terre tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: There are, in our belief, better ways to stabilize the city's budget, but our decades of experience on tax policy reinforce the importance of high-quality tax administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Looking more specifically at the challenges, first, the legislation received limited public vetting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: The bill language was released just one day before the state legislature voted, leaving little opportunity to identify ambiguities and implementation challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Greater vetting would not have prevented all issues, but would have improved the odds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Second, DOF is implementing a new and administratively complex tax with less than eight months from enactment to revenue connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: The law requires determinations about values, ownership, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: residency, including special rules for co-ops and condos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: To meet the deadline, DOF developed regulations and administrative processes in less than seven weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: This time constraint makes the desired analytics, consideration of public input, and communication harder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Third, the city's public education and communications were insufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Many did not understand that the law directed DOF to quote unquote, open to the public the books of annual records of market values of covered properties, which is a much broader group than those subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: DOF chose to comply by publishing the supplemental rule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: This choice appears reasonable, but it did also create near instant confusion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Notably, adequate vetting of the legislation may have helped inform the public or led to a change in the legislation itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Also, DOF did publish more variables than were required and did not indicate whether properties might be subject to the tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Concerns about public disclosure of private information are understandable, but potentially misplaced as the information is already public in the tax roll in the Pluto database in ACRES in numerous sources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: The city should have communicated about the 17,000 letters more clearly, who would receive a letter, why DOF needed additional information, and the next steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Given this confusion, the city was right to extend the deadline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: In addition to lessons noted above,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: the city should take this ideal opportunity to evaluate the pied-a-terre's tax impact on property values, transactions, housing supply, ownership patterns, and tax revenues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: These findings would enable the legislature to smartly adjust the policy if it generates unintended consequences, while also informing comprehensive property tax reform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: The city could also evaluate broader related impacts of changes in supply and ownership, not just on property taxes, but all revenues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ann Rothman
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Leonard Steinberg, a real estate professional and immigrant, calls the tax rollout unfair and punitive. He argues the messaging around $1 million market value is misleading and divisive, and asks the mayor and council to issue a public apology to New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Leonard Steinberg testifies on unfair messaging and calls for public apology

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: My name is London Steinberg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: I am in the real estate world, and I was a little kid in Africa at the age of 20, dreaming of coming to the United States of America, specifically because of the dream of fair and equal treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That is what is specified in the Constitution of the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Everything about the rollout of this tax has been pretty unfair and unequal and extremely punitive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: And I speak to all of you here, and I thank you, especially for those of you who were capable of showing up to something this important, because I think there's a misnomer about the numbers, and I'm going to look at some of the numbers today, but the messaging around this tax is outrageous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: And I'll give you some examples of just how outrageous it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Even in today's discussion, there was mention of this tax applying to apartments and co-ops, condos and co-ops, worth a million dollars or more, with a market value of a million dollars or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That is the message that has been sold to the entire United States of America.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: All New York citizens

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: and around the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That is a false statement, because the market value that the city applies to a property is not the market value that most people would assume is market value, what it would sell for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That means that statement is grotesquely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Secondly, we could talk about this being exposed to over 900,000 homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Yes, but it applies how many people live in each one of these homes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Three?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That amounts to about 3 million New Yorkers out of 8 million New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That's about 40% of the population you are alienating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: But the messaging around this is so divisive and anger-fueling, and it stands in sharp contrast to the message we've been given about uniting the city and bringing us together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: New York City is the dream of people around the world, just like myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: I dreamed of this city and I dreamed of this country because it was inclusive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: It embraced everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Here you have something that is specifically and purposefully aimed at dividing, fueling anger and division.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: That is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: So what I'm asking today is for the mayor and for the city council to group together and come out with an apology to all New Yorkers, because it's every single one of us in this room who pay taxes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Yes, 900 plus thousand people pay a lot of real estate taxes, but everyone in this room pays sales tax and a whole host of other taxes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: And this city hall is paid for by the taxpayers of this room and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: to do the job of the people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: And the people of New York demand that New York City is represented by its mayor and city hall as the bastion of desire throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: The world should crave to be in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: This sends the exact opposite message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: So I'm asking for a great, beautiful...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Video that comes out on social media because this is a very social media savvy group to apologize to all New Yorkers and to clarify the message to the world that no we are not aimed at dividing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: but we're actually aimed at uniting the people of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leonard Steinberg
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, no, thanks.

chapters.summary: Heather Domi, a real estate broker, highlights unintended consequences including retired people, deceased trusts, renovations, and rental properties being swept up. She points to valuation inequalities where a $21M property has a lower estimated market value than a $3M property.
chapters.title: Heather Domi testifies on unintended consequences and valuation flaws

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Heather Domi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: I am a resident of District 1, and I'm very grateful to be here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: I am a real estate broker, have been for 20 years, and I'm grateful to the committee here, council members, for taking this issue with such seriousness and personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: I'm going to talk about the unintended consequences because we haven't gotten to any of that, and that's really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: And I do want to make sure we don't lose fact that this was meant to target homes above $5 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: And as Leonard Steinberg pointed out, the estimated market value of $1 million is what tends to get swept up in the conversation, and we're losing fact that this was meant to target above $5 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: There is an inequality in our system of estimated market value, point-blank examples of an apartment at 15 Central Park West that closed for $21 million

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: in June and a $3 million condo on the Bowery that closed for $3 million in May.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: The property that is seven times the amount of the other one has a lower estimated market value than the $3 million property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: So the system is so incredibly flawed in the way that it is valuing these properties that it is targeting all of the wrong people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: We are targeting, this is targeted retired people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: This is targeted people who have bought from deceased trusts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: So there's no one to claim residency for the January 5th date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: People going through renovations who are here full time, but they can't claim residency to the property because it's unlivable, uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: Owners who have rented their properties out, they've made investments in our city and paid taxes for years, and they put tenants in their property who have long-term leases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: Maybe those people aren't full-time residents, but guess what?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: They're stuck in a lease with a person who's not a full-time resident, so now they're going to have to also pay the pied-a-terre tax on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: So the unintended consequences and the cases are so wide and so vast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: A client who's retired, exited the city, selling their property, and now they have to contest the tax, but by the time the property sells and closes, they will no longer own it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: Will the city honor the fact that this property isn't worth more than $5 million and that they sold the property, and will they get credited back that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: So there's so much uncertainty, so much fear that has been created within.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: New Yorkers who have lived here, invested here, that it really has to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: So many different cases, trusts that weren't set up with this tax in mind, LLCs with joint partners that own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: This structure and the cases need to be examined very closely.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Don't forget about the in-laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Heather Domi
utterances.text: In-laws, too.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: Susan Peters of the American Monetary Institute discusses the root cause of city distress as the U.S. monetary system, arguing that commercial banks privately create money through loans. She cites Bank of England research on money creation in the modern economy.
chapters.title: Susan Peters testifies on monetary system and private bank money creation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Susan Peters, and I'm a resident of the Upper West Side of Manhattan and a member of the American Monetary Institute, a 30-year-old monetary reform 301c3.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I speak today about the root cause of distress in our city, displayed today by our need to legislate a pie-a-terre tax, a wealth tax.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: The root cause is our U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Monetary system, which determines the creation and distribution of money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Who creates all the money our citizens need to live?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Who decides who will receive that money?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I worked for 17 years as a data professional for a Wall Street bank.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I learned the secret of private banking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Our money, the money we all need to pay rent,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: buy food, clothe our family, send our children to school, is privately created by commercial banks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Quote, every time a private commercial bank makes a loan, it creates the loan principal by writing a bookkeeping entry for the principal in the borrower's checking account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: This is new money creating the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Money supply, all from debt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Legally, the banks can charge interest and foreclose on property when the borrower defaults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: This is a vast power in the hands of private parties, not taught in our schools or discussed in our media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: These private banks are deciding who gets loans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Therefore, deciding who gets loans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Deciding who gets loans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: the distribution of our money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: As any citizen can see, the loans are going to the financial economy, which creates stocks and bonds bubbles and ignores the real economy where we all live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Real infrastructure in our city suffers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I'd like to give you some documentation here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: One of them is an article from 2014 published by the Bank of England, which has the same system as ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: The title is Money Creation in the Modern Economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Quote, this article explains how the majority of money in the modern society is created by commercial banks making loans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: End quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Number two, quote, in the modern economy, most money takes the form of bank deposits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: But how those bank deposits are created is often misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: The principal way is through commercial banks making loans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit in the borrower's bank account

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: thereby creating new money.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Please contact me with questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wong asks the Citizens Budget Commission about the tax's five-year sunset clause creating fiscal instability. Champaney agrees it's a fiscal risk, notes many sunset taxes get extended, and says revenue yield remains unknown.
chapters.title: CM Wong questions CBC on five-year sunset clause and revenue stability

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have a question about Citizens Budget Commission.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We have, this tax is a five-year sunset clause.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How does the CBC assess the risk on this five-year sunset clause ending?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: after fiscal year 2031.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That creates, would that create instability from the city?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: He's revenue planning and would CBC recommend any reauthorization or phase out framework right now?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: I think it really depends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Having a tax that sunsets and is temporary arguably is not the sort of recurring revenue that you would want to base your budget on long term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: So it is a fiscal risk that it is set to sunset, though we have seen that many taxes set to sunset in Albany get repeatedly extended.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: So I think there is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: That possibility, I also do think there is a question about comprehensive property tax reform, and if that were to take place, how that would interact with this tax going forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: But I do think you do raise a good question about long-term planning with regards to a tax that will sunset.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: And we really do yet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: Have to wait to see how much revenue it will yield.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Champany
utterances.text: So that's an unknown as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.title: CM Morano questions panel on options for letter recipients and legal costs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.text: That is actually did everything they're supposed to do, like this young man said, coming.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Whomever wants to join us, are you all here?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right, whomever would like to start, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You've got to push the button.

chapters.summary: Beverly Solo, a grandparent of public school teachers, supports the pied-à-terre tax and wants revenue directed to schools and child care. She argues taxing the rich is popular among working New Yorkers and those with luxury second homes should contribute to the city's well-being.
chapters.title: Beverly Solo testifies in support of tax for schools and child care funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: My name is Beverly Solo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: I live in Inwood in northern Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: I've lived in New York City for 44 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: I'm a grandparent and a parent of two public school teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: I'm also a lactation consultant and have worked to help countless new parents return to the workplace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: I'm not here to talk about the merits of how this was the rollout or the implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: Clearly, it's been a mess.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: The vast majority of the discussion has been about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
utterances.text: But let's say those problems could be resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beverly Solo
